title.en: Robber Chê and the Liver Stew: The Harangue of the Great Brigand (Zhuangzi)

region.en: The robber-camp south of Mount T'ai (Shandong, China)
region.zh: 泰山之陽盜寨（今山東泰安南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 29, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 29

summary.en: With a band nine thousand strong, Robber Chê ravages the empire, and Confucius — charioteered by Yen Hui — goes to convert him, finding the brigand eating a dish of minced human liver. Chê's harangue turns every table: Yao and Shun got the empire, yet their descendants have not territory enough to insert an awl's point; you are the biggest thief I know of — if the world calls me Robber Chê, it most certainly ought to call you Robber Ch'iu. Confucius three times misses the reins, having cauterized himself without being ill and very nearly got into the tiger's mouth.
summary.zh: 孔子與柳下季為友；柳下季之弟名曰盜跖。孔子往見之，盜跖乃方休卒徒太山之陽，膾人肝而餔之——若以利惑其真而強反其情性，詩書發塚！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the spurious-but-canonical Robber Chê dialogue is Zhuangzi's great trickster-narrative. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Robber Chê had a band of followers nine thousand strong. He ravaged the whole empire, plundering the various nobles and breaking into people's houses. He drove off oxen and horses. He stole men's wives and daughters. Family ties put no limit to his greed. He had no respect for parents nor for brothers. He neglected the worship of his ancestors. Wherever he passed, the greater States flew to arms, the smaller ones to places of safety. All the people were sore distressed.

The latter had just encamped to the south of T'ai-shan, and was engaged in devouring a dish of minced human liver. Confucius alighted from his chariot, and advancing addressed the doorkeeper as follows:--"I am Confucius of the Lu State. I have heard of the high character of your captain." When Robber Chê heard who it was, he was furious. His eyes glared like stars. His hair raised his cap from his head as he cried out, "What! that crafty scoundrel Confucius of Lu? Go, tell him from me that he is a mere word-mongerer. That he talks nonsense about Wên Wang and Wu Wang. That what he says is mostly rhodomontade. That he consumes where he does not sow, and wears clothes he does not weave. That his lips patter and his tongue wags. Tell him that he deserves the worst, and that if he does not take himself off his liver shall be in my morning stew."

"Ch'iu! come here," cried Robber Chê in a great rage. "There is no State bigger than the empire. Yao and Shun both got this, yet their descendants have not territory enough to insert an awl's point. T'ang and Wu Wang both sat upon the Imperial throne, yet their posterity has been obliterated from the face of the earth. Was not this because of the very magnitude of the prize? ... And now you come forward preaching the old dogmas of Wên Wang and palming off sophistries without end, in order to teach future generations. You are the biggest thief I know of; and if the world calls me Robber Chê, it most certainly ought to call you Robber Ch'iu.

"Ch'iu! all your teachings are nothing to me. Begone! Go home! Say no more! Your doctrine is a random jargon, full of falsity and deceit. It can never preserve the original purity of man. Why discuss it further?" Confucius made two obeisances and hurriedly took his leave. On mounting his chariot, he three times missed hold of the reins. His eyes were so dazed that he could see nothing. His face was ashy pale. ... "He did," said Confucius. "I am a man who has cauterized himself without being ill. I hurried away to smooth the tiger's head and comb out his beard. And I very nearly got into the tiger's mouth."

title.en: Nest-Builders, the Provident, and the War Whose Blood Flowed a Hundred Li (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 有巢氏、知生氏與涿鹿之戰（莊子）

region.en: Chŏ-lu, the battlefield of the Yellow Emperor and Ch'ih Yu (Zhuolu, Hebei, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 29, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 29

summary.en: In Robber Chê's mouth, the great cultural myths are turned into an indictment: in olden times birds and animals outnumbered man and he built his domicile in trees — hence the name Nest-builders; the people did not know how to make clothes and warmed themselves by fire — hence the name Provident; in Shên Nung's days a man knew his mother but not his father and lived among the wild deer. Then the Yellow Emperor fought with Ch'ih Yu at Chŏ-lu, and blood flowed for a hundred li — ever since T'ang and Wu Wang we have had none other than disturbers of the peace.
summary.zh: 古者禽獸多而人民少，於是民皆巢居以避之；晝拾橡栗，暮棲木上，故命之曰有巢氏之民。古者民不知衣服——故命之曰知生之民。黃帝不能致德，與蚩尤戰於涿鹿之野，流血百里。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Robber Chê version of China's culture-hero sequence — Nest-builders, fire-warming providents, Shên Nung's age of perfect virtue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "I have also heard that in olden times the birds and animals outnumbered man, and that the latter was obliged to seek his safety by building his domicile in trees. By day he picked up acorns and chestnuts. At night he slept upon a branch. Hence the name Nest-builders.

"Of old, the people did not know how to make clothes. In summer they collected quantities of fuel, and in winter warmed themselves by fire. Hence the name Provident. "In the days of Shên Nung, they lay down without caring where they were and got up without caring whither they might go. A man knew his mother but not his father. He lived among the wild deer. He tilled the ground for food. He wove cloth to cover his body. He harboured no thought of injury to others. These were the glorious results of an age of perfect virtue. "The Yellow Emperor, however, could not attain to this virtue. He fought with Ch'ih Yu at Chŏ-lu, and blood flowed for a hundred li. Then came Yao and Shun with their crowd of ministers. Then T'ang who deposed his sovereign, and Wu Wang who slew Chou. After which time the strong took to oppressing the weak, the many to coercing the few. In fact, ever since T'ang and Wu Wang we have had none other than disturbers of the peace."

title.en: Chieh Tzŭ T'ui's Slice of Thigh and the Bridge-Assassin Wei Shêng (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 介子推割股，尾生抱柱（莊子）

region.en: The drowned assignation beneath the bridge (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 橋下之約（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 29, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 29

summary.en: Robber Chê's catalogue of the world's 'virtuous': Chieh Tzŭ T'ui cut a slice from his thigh to feed Wên Wang, then grasped a tree and was burnt to death; Wei Shêng made an assignation with a girl beneath a bridge, the water rose, he grasped a buttress and died; Poh I and Shu Ch'i died of starvation on Mount Shou-yang, their corpses deprived of burial — these four differed in no way from dogs and pigs going about begging to be slaughtered.
summary.zh: 介子推至忠也，自割其股以食文公；尾生與女子期於梁下——水至不去，抱梁柱而死。此四子者無異於磔犬流豕。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Among those whom the world calls virtuous were Poh I and Shu Ch'i. They declined the sovereignty of Ku-chu and died of starvation on Mount Shou-yang, their corpses deprived of burial. "Pao Chiao made a great show of virtue and abused the world in general. He grasped a tree and died. "Shên T'u Ti, when no heed was paid to his counsels, jumped into the river with a stone on his back and became food for fishes.

"Chieh Tzŭ T'ui was truly loyal. He cut a slice from his thigh to feed Wên Wang. Afterwards, when Wên Wang turned his back upon him, he retired in anger, and grasping a tree, was burnt to death. "Wei Shêng made an assignation with a girl beneath a bridge. The girl did not come, and the water rose. But Wei Shêng would not leave. He grasped a buttress and died. "These four differed in no way from dogs and pigs going about begging to be slaughtered. They all exaggerated reputation and disregarded death. They did not reflect upon their original nature and seek to preserve life into the old age allotted."
